title: Who Gets to Write?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · Technology, access and voice
objective: Students will read the exhibition’s poster *The Writing Revolution* as a history of access: who could write and be read, and how each new technology — the printing press, the typewriter, the word processor, desktop publishing, the internet — opened the gates wider. They will use the typewriter and the women who became typists to define **democratization**, weigh the new challenges the poster names (information overload, misinformation, and algorithms that decide what writing gets seen), and judge the poster’s own closing claim.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Who gets heard has always depended on who controls the tools of writing. Knowing how that changed helps you ask who controls them now.

items.text: trace how each writing technology, from the printing press to social media, opened writing to more people
items.question: trace how each technology opened writing to more people?

items.text: explain what *democratization* means, using the typewriter and the women who became typists
items.question: explain democratization, with the typewriter as an example?

items.text: name the new challenges the exhibition says came with the power to publish
items.question: name the new challenges that came with the power to publish?

items.text: judge the poster’s claim that every new technology has chipped away at the gates, with evidence for and against
items.question: judge whether every technology really chipped away at the gates?

materials: The *Who could write?* timeline on page 3, projected or printed
The poster *The Writing Revolution*, on screen at the exhibition or printed
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** read *The Writing Revolution*, then find the display case, which holds a portable Smith-Corona Galaxie typewriter and an Apple iMac G3. At the Typing Station, type the same line on both. Which machine made it cheaper and easier to write, and why?

steps.title: A privilege
script: Put the poster’s first sentence on the screen and read it aloud: *“For thousands of years, writing was a privilege reserved for scribes, monks, and the wealthy elite.”* Ask: *“Who got to write, and who didn’t?”* List the excluded groups students name. Then: *“The poster says every new technology chipped away at that. Today you test whether it’s true.”*

screen.text: For thousands of years, writing was a privilege reserved for scribes, monks, and the wealthy elite.

steps.purpose: Open with the poster’s first sentence: writing as a privilege, and the question of who was shut out.
students: Who got to write, and who didn’t?
Who decides who gets to write today?

steps.title: The gates fall
script: Walk through the timeline on page 3. For each row ask: *what was the barrier — cost, skill or permission — and who could now get past it?* Name the poster’s word: **democratization**, opening something once held by a few to everyone.

Stop at the typewriter: *“But true democratization began with the typewriter. Women especially embraced this technology, flooding into offices as typists and gaining economic independence previously denied to them.”* Ask why a writing machine could change who earned a living.

screen.caption: The gates, one technology at a time, as the poster tells it

cells: Writing was a privilege reserved for scribes, monks, and the wealthy elite.
Books cost a fraction of their previous price, sparking mass literacy movements across Europe.
Ordinary citizens could create professional documents; women flooded into offices as typists.
Anyone could edit and perfect their writing without costly reprints.
Anyone could design newsletters, magazines, or books from their home.
Millions published free; collective amateur writers rivaled encyclopedias.
Every phone owner a publisher; authors reach readers without agents or publishing houses.

steps.purpose: Walk the timeline: each technology lowered a barrier of cost, skill or permission.
students: For each row: what barrier fell?

steps.title: New gates?
script: Then read: *“In 1900, only major newspapers and publishers could spread ideas widely; today, a tweet from a teenager can influence millions. Yet this power brings new challenges: information overload, the spread of misinformation, and algorithms that decide what writing gets seen.”* Ask: *in 1900, who were the gatekeepers? Who, or what, are they now?*

screen.text:
In 1900, only major newspapers and publishers could spread ideas widely; today, a tweet from a teenager can influence millions.
Yet this power brings new challenges: information overload, the spread of misinformation, and algorithms that decide what writing gets seen.

steps.purpose: Turn the story: the power to publish brought new problems, and new gatekeepers.
students: Who, or what, decides what writing gets seen today?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the same timeline and the same poster sentences.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Complete the timeline from a word bank, explain what the typewriter meant for women, and put one of the new challenges in their own words.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Fill the timeline’s *what opened up* column, compare the gatekeepers of 1900 and today, and argue which technology was the biggest leap.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh evidence for and against *every new technology has chipped away at the gates*, trace what stayed the same, and predict, as a historian, what AI writing tools will change.

steps.purpose: Work with the timeline and the poster’s claims at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same timeline and the same poster.

steps.title: Still missing?
script: Ask the exhibition’s own question: *“Writing was once only for a few people. Who do you think gets to share their ideas today, and whose voices might still be missing?”* Take answers that use evidence from the timeline; ask Red Level students for their verdict on the poster’s claim.

screen.question: Writing was once only for a few people. Who do you think gets to share their ideas today, and whose voices might still be missing?

steps.purpose: Bring the history into the present, in the exhibition’s own question.
students: Use one piece of evidence from the timeline.
Name one barrier that still stands.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
